The most interesting thing about this election, from my perspective, has been the discussions surrounding the Electoral College; watching people be hypocrites, notice their own hypocrisy (or not), and just keep on moving without breaking stride at all. How quickly we forget, and how well we deceive ourselves.

Every single partisan in this country is failing to reason from consistent principals (when they aren't failing to reason entirely): the country is a democracy at times when such a perspective is politically beneficial, the will of the Framers matters at times when such a perspective is politically beneficial, etc.

"You," below, is a hypothetical "you;" not you the reader.

If you were on the right, you probably celebrated when Trump won the Electoral College, despite losing the popular vote; you may even have celebrated the institution as proper for a Republic, and the protector of real America from the out-sized influence of a few cities (never mind asking if the Electoral College actually solves that problem, or why some people's votes should count more than others'... "this country isn't a democracy after all, that's how the Framers intended it."). Then, when you started to hear murmurs about faithless electors, you probably bristled at the thought of a small group of elites defying the will of the People, and would reject any argument that the Electoral College was designed this way ("Where's my democracy?" Please notice that traditionalism and republicanism are a little scarce in this point of view). The Electoral College giveth, and the Electoral College taketh away (or so you would worry).

If you were on the left, you probably bristled when Clinton won the popular vote but lost the Electoral College; you may have even denounced the institution as undemocratic ("Where's my democracy?" Never mind asking why a pure, popular election might or might not be desirable in a Republic). Then, when you started to hear that in many states electoral voters aren't bound to vote in accordance with the popular vote of their state, you probably started cheering for faithless electors, and you will probably like hearing arguments that this function of the Electoral College--final vetting of the People's choice--is part of its intended design (please notice how undemocratic this view is... "this country isn't a democracy after all, that's how the Framers intended it."). The Electoral College taketh and the Electoral College giveth back (or so you would hope).

We have to start seeing our own hypocrisy, and stop thinking on such short-term bases.
